power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Designing Around the Human Creative Core: A Construct for Preserving Creative Agency in Human-AI Systems

author.affiliation:
Faculty of Instructional Technologies
								Holon Institute of Technology (HIT)
								
									Holon
									Israel

text.text: Generative AI can increasingly perform the parts of professional work where a person's judgment and sense of identity are most engaged.
The common design instinct is to automate wherever AI can plausibly take over, treating capability as the test.
This efficiency-first instinct can erode the skill, judgment, ownership, and professional identity.
Human-Centered AI frameworks show how to structure collaboration and keep people in control, but not which elements of a given workflow sustain a person's creative agency.

This paper introduces the Human Creative Core: the subset of workflow elements where a person's cognitive contribution and psychological investment converge, identified through four dimensions, strategic intention, signature judgment, identity and ownership, and developmental function.
The construct yields a design principle, complement the core and automate the periphery, and a method for locating the core in a given workflow.
The method was taught and applied in a graduate instructional design course, and is demonstrated here across five professional cases.
The contribution is a design construct and a repeatable method for building AI that preserves, and can strengthen, a person's creative agency rather than dissolving it.

A litigation lawyer with fifteen years in civil and administrative practice spends much of his time on tasks he would gladly delegate: sifting discovery for the one inconsistency that matters, cross-referencing exhibits, formatting citations, rebuilding a chronology from documents that arrive partial and out of order.
A generative system can now do most of this in minutes.
The same system can also draft his pleadings and shape the strategic argument.
Constructing that argument is the part that makes him a litigator.
It reflects his reading of the tribunal, his sense of which claims to lead with, and his direction over the case, and it rests on judgment he is accountable for.
An efficiency-first AI design might seek to automate both the sifting and the argument.
This paper asks what that costs to the practitioner's agency, skill and identity, and how a designer could decide in advance which parts to automate and which to keep with the person.
AI now enters work that calls for judgment, expertise, and creative effort.
This comes with costs in skill, judgment, ownership, and sometimes even a practitioner's sense of professional identity.
AI assistance can speed the decay of expert skill and slow its acquisition, often without the person noticing (Macnamara et al., 2024).
text.formatted: AI assistance can speed the decay of expert skill and slow its acquisition, often without the person noticing <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Macnamara et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Knowledge workers using generative AI shift their effort from solving to checking, and report investing less in critical thinking as their trust in the tool grows (Lee et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Knowledge workers using generative AI shift their effort from solving to checking, and report investing less in critical thinking as their trust in the tool grows <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lee et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The same shift from doing to supervising now shows up in fields once thought safe from it, from medicine to software (Greengard, 2025).
text.formatted: The same shift from doing to supervising now shows up in fields once thought safe from it, from medicine to software <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Greengard, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Studies of moral decision-making find that the sense of agency itself weakens as the autonomy of the system rises (Salatino et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Studies of moral decision-making find that the sense of agency itself weakens as the autonomy of the system rises <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Salatino et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These studies surface a pattern which suggests that AI systems and human-AI workflows designed to achieve maximum optimization of outcome or time, can erode the conditions that keep human capability intact.
Human-Centered AI offers a strong answer to part of this problem.

It shows how high automation and strong human control can coexist rather than trade off (Shneiderman, 2020), provides guidelines for human-AI interaction (Amershi et al., 2019), and models the kinds of interaction a co-creative system can support (Rezwana & Maher, 2023).
text.formatted: It shows how high automation and strong human control can coexist rather than trade off <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Shneiderman, 2020)</ref>, provides guidelines for human-AI interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amershi et al., 2019)</ref>, and models the kinds of interaction a co-creative system can support <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rezwana & Maher, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This body of work is about the structure of collaboration and who holds control.
It keeps the person in the loop, able to direct, approve, and adjust what the system does.

But a person can keep that control while the thinking that defined their expertise moves to the system. Dix et al. (2024) name the worry when they warn against designs that leave people as cogs in the machine.
text.formatted: But a person can keep that control while the thinking that defined their expertise moves to the system. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dix et al. (2024)</ref> name the worry when they warn against designs that leave people as cogs in the machine.

text.text: Holding authority over a workflow is necessary, but on its own it does not sustain the motivation, ownership, and developing skill that creative work rests on.
What is missing is a way to decide, element by element, where AI should reach and where it should stop, so that skill, identity, and a person's creative agency stay intact.
This paper treats creative agency as a design objective in its own right, and offers three contributions toward it.

The first is the AI-Creative Agency Framework (Barak-Medina, 2025; Watkins & Barak-Medina, 2024), which explains how a person's perception of an AI shapes whether working with it strengthens or weakens their agency.
text.formatted: The first is the AI-Creative Agency Framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barak-Medina, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Watkins & Barak-Medina, 2024)</ref>, which explains how a person's perception of an AI shapes whether working with it strengthens or weakens their agency.

text.text: The second, and the central concept this paper introduces, is the Human Creative Core (HCC), a construct that identifies the workflow elements a person experiences as the substance of their practice.
The third is an agency-aware workflow analysis, a method for locating the HCC in a given workflow.
The paper covers the construct, its grounding, the method, and demonstrates its application through five cross-domain cases from a graduate design course where the method was developed and taught.

The AI-Creative Agency Framework offers a map that arranges the relationship between how AI functionalities and capabilities are perceived by people, whether correctly or not, and their creative agency.
The HCC builds directly on this framework.

Creative agency is a person's motivation, sense of ownership, and accountability when facing challenges that demand high-level cognitive effort, such as creative production, complex decisions, and problem-solving.
It is task-specific and dynamic.
The same person can hold strong creative agency over one part of their work and little over another.

It is related to the concept of creative self-efficacy, the belief that one can produce creative outcomes (Karwowski et al., 2019; Tierney & Farmer, 2002), yet adds ownership and accountability as components to it.
text.formatted: It is related to the concept of creative self-efficacy, the belief that one can produce creative outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Karwowski et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Tierney & Farmer, 2002)</ref>, yet adds ownership and accountability as components to it.

text.text: The framework is built on two assumptions.
First, an AI's effect on creative agency runs through how the person perceives what the system does, not through what it objectively does.
Second, that perception is task-specific.
The same system can feel like a welcome assistant on one element and a threat on another.
A person's experience with a system, realizing what it can or cannot do, changes their perception and therefore its effect on creative agency.
The framework names four factors that shape whether adding AI to a workflow strengthens or weakens agency:
The first is whether the person sees the system as competing with their skills or complementing them.
This is a perceptual distinction, not a technical one.

It matters because complementary performance, where the human and the system together do better than either alone, is harder to reach than is often assumed (Hemmer et al., 2025), and how the person sees the system is part of what decides whether it is reached.
text.formatted: It matters because complementary performance, where the human and the system together do better than either alone, is harder to reach than is often assumed <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hemmer et al., 2025)</ref>, and how the person sees the system is part of what decides whether it is reached.

text.text: The second is perceived effectiveness, how capable the person judges the system to be, against themselves and their professional community, in speed, accuracy, scope, or consistency.
It sharpens the first.
A competing system the person believes is highly effective is the most threatening to creative agency.
A complementing system believed to be effective is the most strengthening.
The third is stakes, the cost of error in the task at hand.
High stakes raise the pressure to defer to whatever is most reliable.
Low stakes ease it, especially when the value of the activity for the person is in the doing rather than the outcome.
The fourth factor is the person's AI literacy, which includes the mindset they bring to using AI.
The framework names four such mindsets (Barak-Medina, 2025; Watkins et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The framework names four such mindsets <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barak-Medina, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Watkins et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A person can use AI to reach what neither they nor the machine could manage alone (empowerment), hand a task over for the system to perform in their place (delegation), stay away from it due to lack of proficiency, or because of value-driven resistance (avoidance), or set it aside on purpose, knowing it could help in the task at hand, to protect their enjoyment of the work or to keep building a skill (suspension).
These are not fixed traits.
A person can move between them, and the design of the system can encourage one over another.
Figure 1 summarizes the framework.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> summarizes the framework.

text.text: The framework gives a clear test.
AI that a person perceives as complementing and effective is the most likely to strengthen creative agency.

When applying this framework to designing AI systems with the aim of preserving human creative agency, that test helps a designer judge how an AI usage existing or discussed will impact creative agency.
What it does not do is say where in a workflow AI should go in the first place.
Workflow elements differ in what they mean to the person.
Some hold the person's identity, motivation, and developing skill.
Others are tolerated, or actively resented.
Deciding where AI belongs needs a construct that tells the two apart, and that takes in what perception alone leaves out, such as the slow erosion of skill.
The HCC is that construct.
The HCC is the set of workflow elements where a person's cognitive contribution and psychological investment converge.
It is the part of a workflow the person experiences as the essence of what they do, where their skill and judgment are most engaged, and sometimes the reason they entered the occupation.
The core may be a small cluster of elements or a single point in the workflow.
It is a feature of the task and the person, not of any AI, and it asks what an element does for the person whether or not a system is present.
An element belongs to the core when it engages one or more of four dimensions.

The first is strategic intention, the elements of a workflow where the person sets the direction of the work, defining the problem, shaping the solution, and fixing the standard a good outcome has to meet.

In professional practice it is what Schön called problem setting, naming what the problem is and what would count as resolving it, the move that shapes everything the practitioner does next (Schön, 1983).
text.formatted: In professional practice it is what Schön called problem setting, naming what the problem is and what would count as resolving it, the move that shapes everything the practitioner does next <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Schön, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: In creative and research work, the act of finding and formulating the problem, more than solving one already posed, is what distinguishes original work (Getzels & Csikszentmihalyi, 1976).
text.formatted: In creative and research work, the act of finding and formulating the problem, more than solving one already posed, is what distinguishes original work <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Getzels & Csikszentmihalyi, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: When a researcher decides which question is worth pursuing and what would count as a convincing answer, that is strategic intention.
The data gathering and analysis that follow only carry it out.

A finding that can suggest AI might threaten strategic intention is one in which students who wrote with a chatbot produced stronger immediate work but did less of the goal-setting and self-evaluation that would exert their influence on the produced work (Fan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A finding that can suggest AI might threaten strategic intention is one in which students who wrote with a chatbot produced stronger immediate work but did less of the goal-setting and self-evaluation that would exert their influence on the produced work <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The second is signature judgment, the element where a person's distinctive, experiencegrounded judgment comes through, where their tacit knowledge and their stamp on the work show.
It expresses accumulated experience, values, and taste.
It does not necessarily mean that it is the person's advantage over the machine.
Much of what makes skilled practice good cannot be fully put into words and is built only through sustained practice (Collins, 2010; Collins & Evans, 2007; Polanyi, 1966; Sennett, 2008).
text.formatted: Much of what makes skilled practice good cannot be fully put into words and is built only through sustained practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Collins, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Collins & Evans, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Polanyi, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Sennett, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: A generative system can produce work that looks and feels like the exact output done with signature judgment, which is what makes the element tempting to automate.
What it cannot supply is the actual reasoning behind the output, the impact of the practitioner's heuristics on the outcome, the reading of a situation that comes from having met many like it.

Writers given AI-generated story ideas produced work that was individually stronger but more alike, the range of directions narrowing as the system's framing stood in for their own (Doshi & Hauser, 2024).
text.formatted: Writers given AI-generated story ideas produced work that was individually stronger but more alike, the range of directions narrowing as the system's framing stood in for their own <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Doshi & Hauser, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The third dimension is identity and ownership.
These are the elements the person experiences as an expression of who they are, so that doing it is what makes the result feel theirs.

People build their professional sense of self around particular practices, not around a job title (Glăveanu & Tanggaard, 2014; Lepisto et al., 2015), which is why, when AI enters creative work, the first worry professionals voice is about identity and value, not efficiency (Hermann et al., 2025; Kyi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: People build their professional sense of self around particular practices, not around a job title <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Glăveanu & Tanggaard, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lepisto et al., 2015)</ref>, which is why, when AI enters creative work, the first worry professionals voice is about identity and value, not efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hermann et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kyi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Ownership grows from three things: control over the process, close knowledge of the task, and investment of oneself in it (Pierce et al., 2001 (Pierce et al., , 2003)).
text.formatted: Ownership grows from three things: control over the process, close knowledge of the task, and investment of oneself in it <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pierce et al., 2001</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Pierce et al., , 2003))</ref>.

text.text: All three weaken when a system generates and the person only edits.

People report not feeling ownership of AI-written text even when they sign their names to it (Draxler et al., 2024), and self-efficacy and meaning drop under passive AI use while active collaboration protects them (Lee et al., 2026; McGuire et al., 2024).
text.formatted: People report not feeling ownership of AI-written text even when they sign their names to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Draxler et al., 2024)</ref>, and self-efficacy and meaning drop under passive AI use while active collaboration protects them <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lee et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">McGuire et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These identity-bearing elements tend to be the enjoyable ones, since enjoyment in creative work attaches to particular features of a task, such as the right level of challenge and the exercise of mastery (Amabile & Pratt, 2016; Csikszentmihalyi, 1990).
text.formatted: These identity-bearing elements tend to be the enjoyable ones, since enjoyment in creative work attaches to particular features of a task, such as the right level of challenge and the exercise of mastery <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Amabile & Pratt, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Csikszentmihalyi, 1990</ref>).

text.text: When a system absorbs that part, output can rise while motivation falls and boredom grows (Wu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: When a system absorbs that part, output can rise while motivation falls and boredom grows <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Wu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The fourth is developmental function.
Doing the element builds or sustains the mastery the task depends on, and adds to the person's skill over time.

Expertise is reached by passing through stages that cannot be skipped (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1986), so an element whose difficulty is the very thing that builds skill belongs to the core even when its immediate output looks minor.

text.text: Hand the finished output to someone who has not gone through that effort and they may never acquire the underlying skill.
High-school students given an unrestricted AI tutor practiced better while they had it and did worse once it was taken away (Bastani et al., 2025).

text.text: A junior lawyer who has every brief drafted for them may never learn to build one.
Much of any workflow is not part of the HCC.
An element can matter to the outcome, or be cognitively hard, and still not engage any of the four dimensions.
Difficulty is not the test, and neither is importance, although these might converge with the core.

Non-core elements of the workflow, or the "periphery", could include the draining work, the routine steps a person would gladly hand off, and the demanding but impersonal tasks that consume time without building skill or supporting identity.
These are the elements to automate.
Automating them can free time and attention to performing the core elements.
The agency-aware workflow analysis is a procedure for finding a person's HCC inside a workflow, when an existing or a potential AI system could be relevant or integrated into it.
Based on this, a designer of an AI system or a human-AI workflow can tell which elements to keep as human and support, and which to automate or offload.
The method has two steps.
The first step breaks the task into its elements.
The second step weighs each element against the four dimensions to identify the core.
It was developed and taught in a graduate instructional design course whose projects supply the cases in Section 5.
The first step breaks the task into its elements: the decisions, the smaller skills, and the phases of the workflow, at a grain fine enough to separate elements that feel different to do.
"Legal work" is too broad to act on.

"Constructing the strategic argument for a particular judge" and "formatting citations to the court's standard" are at the right register, because the person experiences them differently and a system could perform them differently.

The breakdown can come from an interview, an observation, a questionnaire, or a review of the domain's tasks, drawing on cognitive task analysis, an established set of methods for eliciting the structure of expert work (Clark & Estes, 1996; Tofel-Grehl & Feldon, 2013).

text.text: The second step weighs each element two ways.
One is how well a current AI system could perform it, which can be estimated from what today's systems demonstrably do.

The other is what the element does for the person, which is harder to judge, since it depends on how they experience the element and what its loss would cost them, something a task description does not reveal.
A few questions, directed at the practitioner, help bring it out: • Where in this task do you exercise your most demanding professional judgment, and where does your judgment most affect the result?
• Would you still feel like a [profession] if a system did this part for you?
• If you stopped doing this for a year, which skill would you lose?
• Which parts of this do you find most engaging?
These questions are aids, not a list of requirements.
They help reveal what different actions, tasks or skills that comprise a process, do for the person.
An element is part of the HCC when it engages one or more of the four dimensions, whatever an AI system's effectiveness on it.
The rest is periphery, whether the person finds it burdensome, merely routine, or simply part of the process that is not core.
When an element is genuinely in doubt, the safer default is to treat it as core, since automating a core element by mistake is harder to reverse than leaving a peripheral one in the person's hands.

For the most part, the elements that matter most tend to recur across people in the same occupation or sharing the same challenges, and a competent analysis aims for those shared, identity-bearing elements rather than one person's idiosyncrasies.
Consider a graphic designer who produces brand identities for clients.
Breaking the work into stages and subskills, then weighing each for how well a system could perform it and what it means to the designer, separates the core from the periphery.
Developing the central visual concept is core on grounds of signature judgment, since a system that generated it would take what makes the result the designer's own.
Art-directing the execution, the typographic and compositional choices that give the identity its character, is core on the same grounds, since it is where the designer's taste and trained eye show.
What surrounds these can go to a capable system.
Producing sized variations of an approved design is routine and engages no identity.
Sourcing and first-pass editing of stock imagery is something current systems do well and does not draw on the designer's judgment.

text.text: The element that most needs care is one a system could perform well and that is also part of the HCC.

Automating it would pull the person out of the thinking that sustains their capability, so an AI design that aims at preserving and enhancing creative agency would look to support that element rather than replace it.
An element a system could perform well that is peripheral is a candidate for automation.
Elements a system performs poorly stay with the person by default.
The analysis points to a principle for AI that respects the HCC: complement the core, automate the periphery.
The principle has two parts.

The first concerns the core: Where possible, the design keeps core elements with the person and uses AI to give those elements better conditions, cleaner inputs, better-organized material, or more chances to practise, rather than to perform them.
Support can also take an active form.
A tool can challenge the person's reasoning so they have to defend and sharpen it, as when a system argues the opposing side and the person has to answer it.
The second part is to automate the periphery.
Here the design builds or adapts AI tools to perform that work, so the person no longer has to.
Taken together, the two parts change the question a designer begins with, from what a system can do to what it should do, given what the person needs to stay capable, invested, and accountable.
The method had been applied in a class dealing with designing human-AI hybrid workflows.
The class is part of a graduate program in instructional technologies, performed within a specialty course on AI in learning.

Working in teams of two, students partnered with a practising professional, analyzed that person's workflow, identified the HCC and the periphery, designed a human-AI workflow that supported the core and automated the periphery, and taught the new workflow back to the professional.
The professionals described their own work as collaborators in the projects, not as subjects recruited for a study.

The work process, the designed workflow, including AIpowered solutions the students had designed for the professional, and the aftermath reports of the professionals, had been documented by the student teams.
The paper presents five of these cases, showcasing the application of the analysis method, the identification of the HCC and the resulting design decisions.
The first professional is a litigation lawyer with about fifteen years in civil and administrative practice, running his own firm.
His goal in the workflow studied is case preparation -taking a matter from intake to the documents a court will see.

Interviewing him, the team mapped four stages: intake of the matter, reading and analysis of voluminous pleadings, forming the legal and strategic understanding of the case, and drafting the court documents.
The team identified the core as the construction of the strategic argument for a particular judge: the reading of the tribunal, the ordering of claims, and the narrative that ties the facts together.
This is signature judgment built over years of practice, and the lawyer said it is the part without which he would not feel like a litigator, which ties it to identity and ownership as well.
The surrounding periphery was heavy but held none of that: reading and cross-referencing large document sets, rebuilding chronologies, and formatting citations.
The students built a set of AI tools on the platform the lawyer already used, dividing the work so the system handled processing while the lawyer kept interpretation and decision.
Two of the tools clear periphery.
One maps an uploaded document into claims, evidence, gaps, and a chronology, cutting the initial reading load.
Another arranges the content the lawyer has written into the court's document template.
A third proposes alternative strategic lines with their risks, widening the options he considers without choosing among them.
Opposed to the first two which centered on automating the periphery, this tool is designed to support, not replace, the core.
The fourth tool works on the core as well, and is the one the lawyer valued most.

It is designed as an interactive bot that argues against the lawyer's chosen line like a hostile reader, surfacing weak points, likely cross-examination, and the claims a sceptical judge might reject.
It does not build the argument.
It makes the lawyer build a stronger one.
The strategic argument is never generated for him.
In the framework's terms, the design is complementing rather than competing, the system is capable, and the stakes are high.
The high stakes are what make the complementing design necessary rather than optional.
A bot that drafted the argument would put the lawyer in the supervisory position that erodes judgment over time, signing off on reasoning he no longer built.
Here AI does more than spare him the periphery.
The challenge bot makes his core sharper than it was before, which is the fuller meaning of complementing the core.
Asked to assess the workflow after using the tools on real cases, the lawyer estimated it cut his preparation time by at least thirty percent.
The figure is his own estimate, not a measured result.
The second professional is a senior pedagogical supervisor at a teachers' college, a specialeducation specialist with more than two decades in the field.
She trains student teachers and mentors a small group of newer supervisors.
By the time the project began she described herself as close to leaving.
The administrative load around her work had grown so heavy that she was near burnout, and her departure would have taken years of the college's accumulated knowledge with it.
Interviewing her, the team mapped her work as one central activity, mentoring, surrounded by several administrative burdens.
The team identified the core as mentoring: reading where a developing teacher is, judging what they need next, and guiding them toward it.
This is the element she named as the reason she entered the profession, which places it squarely in identity and ownership.
The periphery was everything that had grown up around it.
She assembled placement schedules by hand from information scattered across messages, calls, and memory.
She answered the same procedural questions again and again, because the answers existed only in her head.

And she rewrote the feedback that newer supervisors drafted for their own student teachers, which was often thin and inconsistent, so that much of her week went to editing other people's reports rather than to mentoring.
The students developed three AI tools, all aimed at the periphery.

A scheduling tool takes structured inputs from students and mentor teachers and produces a draft placement table together with the messages needed to confirm each placement, removing weeks of manual matching.
A question-answering bot, built from her own documented procedures, gives the newer supervisors immediate answers to routine questions and refers genuinely sensitive situations back to her.
A feedback tool takes a newer supervisor's raw observation notes and returns them in that supervisor's own pedagogical format, for that supervisor to approve or revise.
The mechanical work of transcription and formatting is automated, while the evalu-ative judgment stays with the supervisor writing the feedback.
This design does not build a tool for the core.
A core-supporting tool here would be something like a bot that tracked classroom participation to give the supervisor sharper material for her judgment, which was beyond the project's scope.
Clearing the periphery returns the supervisor's time to the mentoring that defines her.
She reported early enthusiasm and beginning use of the tools.
Because the design was new at the time of writing, no outcome beyond that is claimed.

The third professional is an electrical engineer who designs control panels for complex installations, work in which a single wiring error or missing component can cause a short, a fire, or a costly field failure.
Interviewing him, the team mapped his process as three stages: designing the panel's logic, validating the design against its supporting documents, and signing off on it.
The team identified the core as the safety judgment: the engineer reasons through the panel's wiring and logic and can sense that something is wrong before he can fully articulate why.
This is signature judgment of the kind that years of situated practice produce.
The periphery was the validation step before sign-off, a manual, line-by-line cross-check across three documents in different formats, the bill of materials, the wiring list, and the schematic.
It took about a working week per complex panel, and it was the kind of sustained checking in which human attention fades, precisely where a safety-critical discrepancy can hide.
The students developed an AI tool that performs the cross-check, leaving the safety judgment with the engineer.

Built on the organization's existing document platform, it parses the three sources, matches components to connections, and returns only the discrepancies, each with its precise location in the source files.
The tool has been set up to be inclusive of anything that could potentially be a discrepancy.
The engineer decides what every flagged item means.
The tool finds candidates for error but does not certify the panel.

In the trial it flagged two breakers specified at the wrong current rating, an error that would otherwise have surfaced only at installation, and the engineer's review confirmed the discrepancies were real.
Here the stakes are high and the AI tool is highly capable at the peripheral element, yet the design keeps it away from the core.
It feeds the engineer's safety judgment rather than competing with it.
The tireless checking goes to the place where human attention fails, and the decision about what the discrepancies mean stays with the person accountable for the panel.

The engineer reported that validation fell from about five working days to roughly half a day, a self-reported figure from a single project, and said it freed him to do engineering instead of proofreading.
Two further cases show the same method in other domains.
A commercial real-estate consultant leads marketing-mix planning for retail space, including units on a light-rail project.
The team identified her core as the strategic matching of businesses to properties and the negotiation that rests on her personal knowledge of her clients.
The periphery was producing business documents by hand and sorting incoming leads against property attributes.
The students built a document tool that drafts marketingmix files from templates, and a lead automation process that cleans incoming enquiries and ranks candidate matches for her review.
The ranking does more than clear periphery.

No such ranking existed in her workflow before, and its criteria were worked out with her, so it feeds the judgment that is her core, helping her match businesses to properties more sharply than she could unaided.
The AI tools prepare and propose.
She decides, drawing on knowledge of her clients that the system does not hold.
A senior civil engineer manages public-infrastructure megaprojects with a lean team, where decisions and knowledge funnel through one person.
The students identified his core as the strategic coordination and risk judgment he exercises across many interfaces.
The periphery was retrieving knowledge, producing meeting summaries, and answering questions whose answers already existed somewhere.
The students built a project knowledge base that answers questions only from documented sources, and a recording-to-summary pipeline whose output he reviews before release.
He remains the final reviewer of every output.

Over four weeks and five documented meetings he reported that producing a summary fell from between sixty and ninety minutes to five to ten, and retrieving past decisions from one to three hours to a few minutes, both self-reported estimates over a short window.

text.text: In each of the five cases the teams found a small core, offloaded a periphery that had grown heavy, and built the AI so the core stayed with the person, and in several cases so the core was strengthened.

The litigation and engineering cases show the two ways AI can meet a core it could otherwise perform: it can sharpen the core, as the challenge bot does for the lawyer's argument, or feed it, as the discrepancy bot does for the engineer's safety judgment and the ranking bot does for the consultant's matching.
The pedagogy and infrastructure cases show the more common move, clearing a heavy periphery so the professional can put attention back on the elements that form the core.
The recurrence has to be read with care.
The teams shared a method and an instructor, so it shows that the analysis can be taught and repeated, not that a profession holds one fixed core waiting to be found.
What it does show is that the line between core and periphery is one a designer can locate and act on, across professions that otherwise have little in common.
The intuitive instinct in designing and implementing AI systems is asking what it can do, and how it can do more or better.
The introduction of the HCC construct offers a slightly nuanced starting point: what should it do, given what the person needs to stay capable and invested.
It adds a procedure for answering that, rather than leaving it to intuition.
The result is a short list of elements to design around, enough to tell efficiency-driven automation apart from a design that leaves the person intact.
The risk that AI erodes human and creative agency is widely discussed.
What is still rare is a way to design for agency, not only to worry about it.
The HCC is meant to be that method.
The HCC responds and adds to existing frameworks and studies in the human-AI interaction field and the human-centered AI tradition.

The COFI framework (Rezwana & Maher, 2023), one of the major pillars of the field, catalogues the interaction choices a co-creative system can make: whether the partners take turns or work in parallel, how the task is divided, who takes the initiative, and how the two communicate.

text.text: It describes how an interaction can be built, but not which of those choices sustain the person's motivation or identity.
The construct supplies that criterion.
Research on human-AI complementarity is about when a person and an AI together do better than either alone.
The advantage comes from two differences between them, in what each knows and in what each can do (Hemmer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The advantage comes from two differences between them, in what each knows and in what each can do <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hemmer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It leaves out what happens to the person's motivation when they see the system as competing with them.
That is what the creative-agency framework addresses and the HCC makes specific.
Research on task allocation (Schemmer et al., 2024) comes closest to the construct.
text.formatted: Research on task allocation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Schemmer et al., 2024)</ref> comes closest to the construct.

text.text: It places AI's role on a continuum from automation to augmentation and shows, for instance, that giving people the hardest, AI-uncertain cases raises a team's overall accuracy.
Both it and the HCC keep some elements with the person, but they sort by different questions.
Task allocation asks who performs a task better.
The HCC asks what the person would lose by giving it up, so an element can stay with them for the sake of identity or development even when a system could do it as well or better.
More empirical work that examines how people experience agency while working with AI is aligned with the dimensions of the HCC.
A think-aloud study of co-creation in image generation and writing watched people manage their sense of control, autonomy, and ownership as they worked (Rafner et al., 2025).

text.text: Complementing the core can do more than keep it with the person.
The cases reported in the article show that a well-designed system can make the person better at the part they most care about.
The challenge bot sharpened the lawyer's argument, and the ranking bot sharpened the real-estate consultant's matching.
The aim is not to protect human work from a more capable machine, but to build a hybrid in which the person stays the author of the core and does it better than before.
This paper proposes designing AI systems and human-AI workflows by assessing how they affect human creative agency.
That could be misread as opposing the drive for more capable AI, or as keeping core elements with the person even when a system would do them better, just to keep agency alive.
It is neither.
The paper does not argue against capable AI, and it does not claim that agency should always win.
It offers a way to assess and design for creative agency, not a rule that it must come first.
There are cases where letting the system take a core element is the right choice, even at a cost to the person's agency.
The clearest is safety.

Where an error can be catastrophic, in surgery, air-traffic control, or critical infrastructure, and a system clearly outperforms human judgment, performance has to come first, and the article does not dispute that.
The construct asks only that this be a deliberate choice, not a default.
The trade-off between machine reliability and human agency should be stated openly, and its long-term costs counted.

Those costs include the skill that fades when a person stops exercising it, the decline in their ability to catch the system's errors, and the risk that builds when the system meets a case outside its training (Bainbridge, 1983; Strauch, 2018).
text.formatted: Those costs include the skill that fades when a person stops exercising it, the decline in their ability to catch the system's errors, and the risk that builds when the system meets a case outside its training <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bainbridge, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Strauch, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Naming the core makes those costs visible when the choice is made, so that giving it up is done knowingly.
The HCC has not been tested.
It offers a way of seeing a workflow, and the claim that its four dimensions converge on the same elements is argued here, not measured.
The cases are demonstrations from a teaching setting.
Their evaluations rest on what the professionals reported in guided conversation, so the reported time savings should be read as how they experienced the change, not as controlled measurements.
Because the teams shared a method and an instructor, the recurrence across cases shows that the analysis can be taught and repeated, not that the same pattern would appear on its own.

One open question is empirical, whether the analysis, applied to different people in the same role, converges on a core stable enough to design products around, and whether pairing the method with established measures of ownership and motivation would sharpen it.
Another is the perceptual claim at the centre of the framework, that the same system helps or harms agency depending on whether the person reads it as complementing or competing.
This could be tested directly, holding the system's actual capability constant while varying how the person sees it.
Both would turn a demonstrated construct into a measured one.
Creative agency belongs among the goals that the design of AI for human work should serve.
This paper has offered three things toward that goal: a lens for seeing creative agency, a construct for locating it inside a workflow, and a method for designing around it.
The claims are calibrated to what the cases can support.
The method can be taught and repeated, and people can locate their own core in conversation.
The construct's dimensions are grounded in established research and the cases demonstrate the method rather than establishing a fixed law of how work divides.
The paper argues that a person's engagement, development, and ownership deserve explicit weight as goals in their own right.
It does not claim they always matter more than efficiency.
As AI grows more capable, more people will find that a system can perform the part of their work they consider most their own.
The question is not whether machines will be able to do it.
It is whether the systems built around them will keep people engaged, developing, and accountable, and, at their best, help people do the part they care about even better than before.
